The rules governing the European Parliament's composition are primarily laid down in Article 14(2) of the Treaty on European Union (TEU). This article stipulates that the European Council, acting unanimously on the initiative of Parliament and with its consent, adopts a decision establishing the composition. It also sets a maximum of 751 representatives (750 Members plus the President) and applies the principle of degressive proportionality. The allocation of seats is further detailed by European Council Decision (EU) 2018/937 [Source: How_the_European_Union_works_2023.pdf, p.68, p.77].

In contrast, the procedures for electing the European Parliament are governed by a combination of European legislation and specific national provisions. Common European rules include the principle of proportional representation, rules on thresholds, and certain incompatibilities with the Member of the European Parliament mandate. However, many other important matters, such as the exact electoral system used and the number of constituencies, are governed by national laws, which vary from one Member State to another. The Act of 20 September 1976 established direct universal suffrage for these elections [Source: How_the_European_Union_works_2023.pdf, p.74].

In summary, the composition rules define the overall structure and size of the Parliament at the EU level, while the electoral procedures involve a blend of common EU principles and diverse national implementations for how MEPs are actually elected.
